text: Why is a stream defined as a one-way sequence of items rather than as random access into a file?
choices: A file's length cannot be known before it is read, so seeking has no meaning.
Sequential access is always faster, so the library removes the slower option.
Random access is impossible on modern solid-state drives, which have no seek operation.
The smaller abstraction also describes a socket, a pipe, and standard input, so code written against it works on all of them.
explanation: A file could be seeked; a network connection has no length at all, and data arrives until it stops. Deliberately offering less means the same `BufferedReader` code works whether the source is a file, a socket, or a string. Chapter 26's `Stream<T>` is the same idea applied to collections — a sequence pulled one element at a time, consumed once, with no going back.
